title: Headings (h1–h6)
description: The h1–h6 elements, heading hierarchy, and why it matters for accessibility and SEO.
subject: html
html:
The heading elements <h1> through <h6> mark the titles of a page and its sections, in decreasing order of importance. They're the backbone of a page's outline — for readers, screen readers, and search engines alike.

Syntax

<h1>Largest / most important</h1>
<h2>...</h2>
<h3>...</h3>
<h4>...</h4>
<h5>...</h5>
<h6>Smallest / least important</h6>

Basic Example

<h1>Learn Data Science</h1>
<h2>What You'll Learn</h2>
<p>Python, SQL, statistics and machine learning fundamentals.</p>
<h2>Who This Is For</h2>
<p>Beginners with no prior programming experience.</p>

Browser output: "Learn Data Science" appears large and bold, followed by two smaller bold section titles, each with its paragraph underneath — no CSS applied yet, just the browser's default heading styles.

How It Works

  1. The browser applies decreasing default font-size and bold weight from <h1> down to <h6> — this is just the User-Agent stylesheet, easily overridden by your own CSS.
  2. Behind the scenes, every heading also builds an entry in the page's document outline — an invisible table-of-contents structure that browsers, screen readers, and search engines all read.
  3. The visual size is incidental. The real job of a heading is to say "a new section starts here, and this is its rank."

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
idTurns the heading into an anchor target — e.g. <h2 id="pricing"> can be linked to with <a href="#pricing">
classHooks the heading for CSS styling — no heading-specific attributes exist beyond the universal global ones

Real-World Example

<article>
    <h1>Complete Guide to SQL Joins</h1>
    <h2 id="inner-join">INNER JOIN</h2>
    <p>Returns only matching rows from both tables...</p>
    <h2 id="left-join">LEFT JOIN</h2>
    <p>Returns all rows from the left table...</p>
</article>

This is exactly how long-form technical articles (like this notes site) are structured — one <h1> for the article title, <h2> for each major topic, giving both readers and search engines a clear map of the content.

Common Mistakes

  • Using more than one <h1> on a page — in practice, browsers and SEO tools still expect exactly one per page, even though the old HTML5 "multiple h1 per section" outline algorithm technically allowed it
  • Skipping levels — going from <h1> straight to <h4> because it "looks right," which breaks the logical hierarchy
  • Choosing a heading level purely because of its default font size, rather than its actual place in the content's structure — use CSS to change how a heading looks, never the tag to fake a font size

Best Practices

  • Exactly one <h1> per page, describing what the whole page is about
  • Nest headings in order — don't skip from <h2> to <h4> without an <h3> in between
  • Write heading text that makes sense read on its own, out of context — that's exactly how screen reader users often navigate

Accessibility Considerations

Screen reader users frequently jump between headings using a single keystroke to build a mental map of the page before reading in full — much like skimming a table of contents. A broken or skipped hierarchy makes that navigation confusing or actively misleading.

SEO Considerations

Search engines use heading structure as a strong signal of what a page is about and how its content is organized. The <h1> typically carries the most topical weight, and a clean <h2>/<h3> hierarchy helps content qualify for rich results like sitelinks and "jump to section" snippets.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

HTML5 originally proposed that sectioning elements (<article>, <section>) could each reset heading levels back to <h1> under an "outline algorithm." No major browser ever implemented that outline, and it was later removed from the spec — so in real-world practice, treat "one visible <h1> per page, in strict descending order" as the rule that actually matters.

Mini Practice

  1. Write a page about your favorite hobby using one <h1> and at least two <h2> sections.
  2. Add an id to one heading and link to it from a "Jump to section" link at the top of the page.
  3. Take a page that jumps from <h1> to <h3> and fix the missing level.
